e.t: Balah is a Hebrew proper name, identifying a named place or person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. It appears only once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Joshua 19:3, and is rendered “Balah.” Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the specific identity of what Balah names must be understood from that passage. Its basic lexical role is therefore a name preserved as “Balah,” not a word translated into an ordinary descriptive term.

This Hebrew verb means “kick,” describing a forceful thrust with the foot and, by extension, resistant or defiant action. In its two Old Testament occurrences, it is rendered “kick” or “kicked,” so the word portrays more than ordinary movement: it conveys pushing back rather than yielding. The word appears once in Deuteronomy and once in 1 Samuel, showing this compact but vivid image in two passages. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding context.

Admatha is a proper name identifying a person, rather than a word that describes an action, quality, or abstract idea. In the Hebrew Bible, it occurs once, in Esther 1:14, and English renderings preserve the name as “Admatha.” Because personal names do not necessarily translate into an ordinary descriptive meaning, the safest sense is the name itself. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic lexical function is to identify an individual.

This Hebrew word functions as a predicate, expressing that a person or thing “is” in a stated condition or description. It helps connect the subject with what is being said about it, rather than naming an object or action by itself. The word occurs 34 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, so its normal force is grammatical and contextual: the surrounding words show what condition or description is being affirmed. Its precise sense in any verse depends on that sentence’s wording.

This Hebrew word means “pit,” referring to a hollow or cavity in the ground. It occurs once in the Old Testament Hebrew corpus, in Ecclesiastes 10:8. In that passage, the word functions as the object associated with falling into, breaking through, or being caught by a pit. Its basic meaning is therefore a physical opening or depression that can present danger to someone near it.

This Hebrew word means “palace.” It points to a place or building identified as a palace rather than expressing an action, command, or quality. The name itself does not function as a general description, action, or quality; it identifies a person within the genealogical and rebuilding records of Israel’s returned community. Its precise significance in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its normal use here is as a person’s name.

This Hebrew word refers to “age,” describing a person’s stage or measure of life. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, at Genesis 48:10. As a noun-like word, it identifies age as a condition or circumstance rather than an action. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning concerns the age associated with a person.

The surrounding verse determines exactly what noun it identifies, but the word itself contributes specificity rather than an independent action or quality.
